blocks.title: How Computers Learn to See
blocks.subtitle: From pixels to objects, scenes and decisions

blocks.text:
To a computer an image is only a grid of numbers. Computer vision is the work of turning those numbers into statements about the world: there is a car here, a person there, this surface is cracked, that tumour has grown.

The field moved from hand-written rules to systems that learn their own features from millions of labelled images.

blocks.heading: What a vision model does
blocks.text: A convolutional network slides small learned filters across the image. Early layers respond to edges and colours, middle layers to textures and parts, and deep layers to whole objects. A task-specific **head** then turns those features into a class label, a set of boxes or a mask.

steps.text: **Classify.** Decide what the image shows as a whole: one label for the entire picture.
**Detect.** Find every object of interest and draw a box around each, with a class and a confidence.
**Segment.** Label every pixel, so the exact outline of each object or region is known.
**Track.** Follow the same objects from frame to frame in video and estimate their motion.

blocks.heading: Data decides
blocks.text: A vision model is only as good as its training data. If the data lack night scenes, unusual viewpoints or certain groups of people, the model will fail on them. Careful dataset design, augmentation and evaluation on held-out, realistic data matter more than small changes in architecture.

blocks.heading: Limits to keep in mind
blocks.text: Vision models can be fooled by small, deliberate changes to an image, and they fail in conditions absent from their training data. Small objects, occlusion, glare and motion blur remain hard. Systems that affect people, such as face recognition, raise questions of bias, consent and oversight that engineering alone cannot settle.

blocks.question: Which task labels every pixel of an image?
blocks.explanation: Segmentation assigns a class to each pixel; detection only draws boxes.

blocks.question: An IoU of 1.0 between a predicted and a true box means:
options: The prediction is twice as large
blocks.explanation: IoU is the area of overlap divided by the area of union, so identical boxes score 1.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Feature map**: the output of a layer of filters. **Anchor**: a reference box a detector adjusts. **Non-maximum suppression**: removing duplicate detections of one object. **Augmentation**: random changes to training images that improve robustness.
